stories.headline: Fantasy hockey rankings: Hellebuyck rises, McDavid still overall leader
stories.summary: Connor Hellebuyck rises, Connor McDavid is still the fantasy hockey rankings leader after his red-hot start.
stories.body:
Halloween came early in New Jersey, where Connor Hellebuyck showed up dressed as a Devil and now sits at No. 66 after missing the top 250 in our last edition. Keeping up the Halloween theme, Dylan Garand turned into a pumpkin between rankings. And the scariest sight in fantasy remains Connor McDavid, projected for about 28 more points the rest of the way than Leon Draisaitl at No. 2.

These rankings are based on expectations of fantasy points produced from Friday, Oct. 30, until the end of the season. stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at Mexico City GP -- or why he may already be champion
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli could be crowned F1 world champion at the Mexico City Grand Prix. Here's what he needs to do to seal his first title.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli inched closer to his first world title after extending his lead in the championship from his two closest rivals George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the United States Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by a whopping 123 points in the standings with a maximum of 125 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he is looking more than likely to be crowned champion on Nov. 1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 75 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would mean Antonelli has already won the title after maximising all the points on offer in Austin.

- Kimi Antonelli wins United States GP but made to wait for first F1 title

- Toto Wolff hails Kimi Antonelli on U.S GP win: 'The race of a champion who isn't a champion yet'

- George Russell: Finishing second in F1 title race 'doesn't mean anything'

Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris were in mathematical contention for this year's championship, but after Austin, they are no longer in the title fight, leaving just Russell and Hamilton still in the mix.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Mexico?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Mexico have now dramatically increased after he converted his Mercedes from pole into his ninth race victory of the season in Austin.

Antonelli would need to finish in ninth place or higher in Mexico to be crowned champion, regardless of where his rivals finish.

If Hamilton wins in Mexico, a 10th place finish for Antonelli would be enough for him to seal the title.

Antonelli needs to score two points, or not be outscored by Russell by 24 points and Hamilton by 25 points. If neither Russell or Hamilton win the race, Antonelli will win the championship regardless of where he finishes.

The reason Antonelli could still win the title despite potentially finishing level on points with Russell or Hamilton -- a scenario possible if Russell wins in Mexico and Antonelli finishes ninth, or Hamilton wins and Antonelli finishes 10th -- is countback, with the Mercedes driver guaranteed to have more race victories than either rival.

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli has already become world champion in Austin, but the final races are still due to go ahead as planned.

The permutations for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Mexico City are:

If Antonelli finishes ninth or higher, he will be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish and even if Russell wins the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion even if Hamilton wins the race.
If Hamilton or Russell don't win the race, Antonelli will be crowned champion no matter where he finishes.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs just two points over the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Global power ranking: The top 20 soccer teams in the world, ranked!
stories.summary: If we look beyond the Premier League and beyond those who qualified for the Champions League, which are the best teams in the world?
stories.body:
Which is the best soccer team in the world?

It might seem easy to answer, and maybe it is. Paris Saint-Germain have won the Champions League two seasons in a row, and they just beat Manchester City and Barcelona, 4-2 in consecutive league-phase matches.

But what about after PSG? Is it Arsenal or Bayern Munich, who just tied each other? Is it Barcelona, who just lost back-to-back games to PSG and Real Madrid? Is it Real Madrid, who are in third place in their league? Is it Manchester City who, uh ... [frantically waves arms toward the 114 charges they were just found guilty of].

And beyond that top tier, are some midtable Premier League clubs better than Champions League qualifiers in Germany? How many English teams would be the favorites to win Serie A? How many Serie A teams would be the second-best team in Germany? And what about, um, Ligue 1?

We will try to address those questions now, and for the rest of the season, with these power rankings of the top 20 teams in the world.

Because any kind of cross-league analytical model would require various, increasingly subjective decisions from me, these instead will be my subjective rankings. In other words, who do I think would win more often if these teams played 100 games on a neutral field?

Along with the rankings below, each team is accompanied by a number of stats from their domestic league: how many points they've won, their non-penalty adjusted goal differential (a blend of 70% expected goals and 30% goals), and the average Opta power rating of their league opponents thus far (not adjusted for home and away).

Now, on to the top 20 list!

1. Paris Saint-Germain

- Points (place): 17, 1st

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.93, 1st

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.3, T-4th

I'm taking a "first place until proven otherwise" approach with PSG after the past two seasons. Over their back-to-back Champions League run, they've been brought to penalties twice -- one in each year -- by the champions of the best league in the world, Liverpool and then Arsenal, and both of those teams required borderline-absurd, conservative, defensive approaches to get there.

The big question from here: How will they cope with losing Khvicha Kvaratskhelia for the season?

2. Bayern Munich

- Points (place): 17, 1st

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 2.42, 1st

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.0, 15th

You could look at their home draw with Arsenal as a negative, given they were -- you know -- at home. But they probably should've won, despite Michael Olise and Joshua Kimmich missing the match and Luis Díaz featuring for just a handful of minutes at the end.

There's a gap, in my mind, between No. 1 and No. 2 in these rankings, but the gulf between No. 2 and No. 3 is the size of "Bukayo Saka being expected to miss a month-plus with a hamstring injury."

3. Arsenal

- Points (place): 21, 2nd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.94, 2nd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 91.9, 17th

Here is one graphic to sum up the state of European soccer. On one axis is each team's adjusted goal differential in their domestic league. On the other is the average Opta power rating of each team's opponents. See if you can spot the Premier League teams:

So, as you grind your teeth about Arsenal's problems in attack, try to remember this: Their average league opponent this season would be ranked 20th in Opta's ratings.

4. Barcelona

- Points (place): 27, 1st

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 2.14, 1st

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.2, T-12th

This team has a higher ceiling than anyone in the world, but well, first this happened:

And then this happened:

In back-to-back games against PSG and Real Madrid, Barcelona conceded 5.75 expected goals (xG) and six actual goals. Arsenal, meanwhile, have conceded five goals -- across eight Premier League matches.

Barcelona's high-flying high-press under manager Hansi Flick will always give up more goals than the other elite teams do, but Barca's defensive personnel isn't at the same level as the three teams ahead of them, either.

5. Real Madrid

- Points (place): 24, 3rd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 1.28, 2nd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 87.2, 4th

The results and the performances have been pretty good so far, but I'm still not sold on the process. Under manager Jose Mourinho, they've controlled just slightly more than half of the final-third possession (field tilt) in LaLiga. That's their lowest mark on record, and the only other time they came close was in the forgettable 2008-09 season under Bernd Schuster and Juande Ramos:

The reactive approach worked well against Barcelona, but will they win enough points against everyone else without tilting the field?

6. Manchester City

- Points (place): 21, 1st

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 1.05, 1st

- Strength of opponent (rank): 92.0, 16th

If we shift our focus just to Man City's on-field worries, then the main one becomes quite clear: They can't really defend all that well.

They're conceding nearly 1.3 xG and over 10 shots per game -- both the highest marks they've allowed over the past 10 years. It seems like the plan was to play Enzo Fernández and Rayan Cherki in the same midfield, but neither defends: Cherki never did, and Enzo doesn't anymore. Elliot Anderson is fantastic -- but he's still not N'Golo Kanté.

7. Liverpool

- Points (place): 15, 4th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.34, 6th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 92.5, T-8th

Using the playing-styles breakdown from Futi, we can see the effect manager Andoni Iraola has already had on the way the team plays:

Essentially, the graphic is organized by how much control of the ball a team has and how aggressively it presses. The days of patient build-up play and constant control are gone, but the pressing remains as aggressive as ever.

And though it hasn't produced a run of dominant performances, they've now beaten four teams in this top 20. The 3-0 loss to City flipped as soon as Ryan Gravenberch got sent off in the second half, so this weekend's match against Arsenal should provide a clearer picture of just how good this team is.

8. Inter Milan

- Points (place): 25, T-1st

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 1.52, 1st

- Strength of opponent (rank): 84.6, 18th

If you're friends with an Inter Milan fan, then you might want to make sure their bathroom is stocked with antacids, they've recently been to the doctor to have their blood pressure checked, and they have more than a passing familiarity with the Eastern philosophical concept of "nonattachment."

For the rest of us? This is the most fun team in Europe now: Inter Milan create a million chances every match, they concede a million chances every match and they either win every game with two goals in injury time or they lose at home to Club Brugge in the Champions League.

9. Atlético Madrid

- Points (place): 25, 2nd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.89, 3rd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.1, T-15th

Though the vibes around Atletico haven't changed -- every game still feels like a knife fight -- the way they play certainly has. They're attempting 18.9 shots per game and are controlling 64% of the final-third possession in their LaLiga matches -- both highs across the Diego Simeone Era.

Only Barcelona are taking more shots and tilting the field more aggressively in Spain.

10. Brighton

- Points (place): 16, 3rd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.92, 3rd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 93.1, 4th

They're leading the Premier League in non-penalty goals, and they're second in the league (behind City) for non-penalty expected goals. And that's without either of Brighton's best attackers, Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh, playing a minute this season. They are not good defensively -- they are barely average on defense -- but the trade-off has easily been worth it so far.

11. AS Roma

- Points (place): 21, 3rd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 1.18, 2nd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.5, T-3rd

They really should've beaten Real Madrid in the Champions League; AS Roma dominated the majority of the match and then capitulated to a couple of set pieces in the final minutes to blow a 3-1 lead and lose 4-3. But manager Gianpiero Gasperini finally has Roma looking like those high-pressing, risk-taking Atalanta teams we all loved. Nearly 10 games in, they are absolutely contenders for the Serie A title.

12. Chelsea

- Points (place): 13, 5th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): -0.02, 9th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 92.5, T-8th

Though their numbers have improved a bit from that bonkers start to the season, you'll see that Chelsea still have a negative adjusted goal differential through the first eight games. Under Xabi Alonso, they continue not to press and they've yet to produce a dominant win that wasn't aided by red-hot finishing in front of goal. If things don't change -- and soon -- the results will get a lot worse.

13. Bournemouth

- Points (place): 9, 13th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.42, 5th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 93.3, T-2nd

I couldn't put Bournemouth ahead of Chelsea because Chelsea beat Bournemouth 5-1. But Bournemouth just played back-to-back games against AC Milan and Manchester United, and Bournemouth won both of those games by a combined score of 6-0. Remember when Milan and Manchester United won the Champions League in 2007 and 2008? Back then, Bournemouth were getting relegated ... to League Two.

After some rotten luck over the first month-plus of the season, Marco Rose's players are finally getting the results that their performances have deserved.

14. Juventus

- Points (place): 14, 7th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.61, 5th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 84.5, T-19th

Remember how fun Luciano Spalletti's Serie A-winning Napoli side was? His Juventus team is ... the exact opposite of that. Spalletti, instead, has the Old Lady looking like the Old Lady of old.

Through nine matches, Juventus have allowed 5.35 expected goals. Across Europe's Big Five top leagues, the next-best mark is Arsenal, at 6.19.

15. Como

- Points (place): 20, 4th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.64, 4th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 85.1, 16th

Compared with last season, Como are attempting a full six more shots per match, and they're generating 0.22 more xG per game. But the trade-off hasn't quite been worth it for manager Cesc Fabregas.

They've also allowed an extra four shots per game and conceded an extra 0.44 xG. In the Champions League, though, the opposite is happening: They've been outshot through three matches, but they've created 2.12 xG per match and conceded just 0.98.

16. Aston Villa

- Points (place): 11, 9th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): -0.41, 16th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 93.3, T-2nd

Are they doing it again? Last season, Villa looked like they might be in a relegation battle after a terrible start to the season -- and then they finished fourth. This season, they took one point in their first four matches and then went win, draw, win, win over the next quartet of games.

Throw in the Champions League, where they're 3-0 and burying their opponents under an avalanche of chances, and it looks even better.

After a couple of years of rough finishing at Chelsea, Nicolas Jackson has seven goals from 31 shots worth fewer than 4.0 xG.

17. Borussia Dortmund

- Points (place): 17, 2nd

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.77, 4th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 85.1, 16th

They continue to be ... just ... fine? Sure, they've allowed just four goals across their first seven Bundesliga matches, but don't expect them to slow down Bayern Munich this weekend in Der Klassiker. Dortmund have conceded 7.3 xG in the league, and they've allowed an even higher mark against a cushy Champions League schedule. Their next two European matches, though: Arsenal and then Inter Milan.

18. Bayer Leverkusen

- Points (place): 13, 4th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.56, 6th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 86.4, 14th

They've been pummeling teams in the Europa League and had rallied back after a shocking opening-day loss to Elversberg, but then this happened against bottom-half-of-the-table Hoffenheim over the weekend:

Am I convinced that this team is better than Brentford -- and a bunch of other Premier League clubs? Absolutely not.

19. Brentford

- Points (place): 11, 6th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.48, 4th

- Strength of opponent (rank): 92.1, T-14th

This is where the rankings get tricky. Implied rankings from the betting odds have Brentford as a stronger team than Dortmund and Leverkusen. But Brentford also just struggled to a 1-1 draw with Hull City, theoretically the weakest team in the Premier League. But also, what does it mean to struggle against the worst team in the Premier League -- on the road -- anymore?

The Bees have given up one more shot than they've allowed through eight matches, and yet, they've turned that into the fourth-best adjusted goal differential in the Premier League. I would love to see Brentford play one of the top teams in any of Europe's other leagues.

20. RB Leipzig

- Points (place): 12, 5th

- Adjusted goal differential (rank): 0.94, 2nd

- Strength of opponent (rank): 87.1, T-6th

Other than getting demolished by Bayern Munich, they've been quite good in the Bundesliga this season. But they've been horrible in the Champions League -- again. Last time they were there, in 2024-25, they won once and lost their other seven league-phase matches. They've already won this year -- progress! -- but they lost their other two matches by a combined scoreline of 8-2.

Though, as always, Leipzig have a bunch of promising prospects, the estimated value of their roster, per Transfermarkt, would rank just 13th in the Premier League.

stories.headline: Kevin Durant reflects on his eight seasons with the Oklahoma City Thunder
stories.summary: After the most acrimonious exit of his career, Durant reveals how much he appreciates Oklahoma City and shares his feelings as the team tries to create a dynasty.
stories.body:
Nearly two decades ago, in July 2008, Kevin Durant arrived in Oklahoma City.

He was 19 years old, in just his second season in the NBA and the new face of a young franchise that had just moved from Seattle.

Though the Thunder started slowly in his first season, the team famously reached the NBA Finals in its fourth season in Oklahoma with a promising young core of Durant, Russell Westbrook and James Harden -- all future NBA MVPs.

The Thunder fell in the 2012 Finals to the Miami Heat, but the team seemed poised for a dynastic run. Yet 2012 marked that core's only Finals appearance in Oklahoma City. All three players moved on, with Durant leaving in 2016 for Golden State, where he won consecutive NBA championships and Finals MVPs with the Warriors.

Years later, in a weird twist of cosmic fate, the Thunder completed what that Durant, Westbrook, Harden core could not: They won a championship.

The Thunder won the 2025 title and are well-positioned to contend for years to come.

Durant, a 19-year veteran, is now in his second season with the Houston Rockets.

After being selected second in the 2007 draft by the Seattle SuperSonics, he played eight seasons in Oklahoma City, and for all the accolades he received there, some in OKC viewed his departure in 2016 with acrimony. He has been welcomed back, at times, with boos.

In an exclusive interview with ESPN's David Seronick for the E60 documentary "The Oklahoma Standard," which details the Thunder's connection to the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum, Durant reflected on his time with the Thunder, the city and the team's 2025 championship.

"I really, really am grateful to be an alumni of the Thunder and to help kick-start this thing off with a lot of my teammates," Durant said. "It's amazing to see. It's tough to play against as a player, but there's still a little side of me when I play against these guys, I've got a soft spot in my heart for that state."

Durant and the Rockets play the Thunder on Oct. 31 in their first meeting of the season.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity:

ESPN: What do you remember about arriving in Oklahoma City in 2008 and how the city greeted you?

Durant: With open arms. The excitement, the energy level was high. We weren't a great team. We were a young team in rebuilding mode. But you wouldn't have thought that from listening and hearing the fans around the city once we got there. You could tell that region was waiting for a professional team to come. And I felt right at home early.

ESPN: The city had been the temporary home of the New Orleans Hornets when that team was displaced by Hurricane Katrina in 2005, but what do you think it meant to fans to have their own team?

Durant: It meant everything. It was finally a way to get out of that dark cloud of the Oklahoma City bombing. Obviously, inside the state of Oklahoma, the community means much more (than that). But outside, people who've never been to Oklahoma, who only heard about Oklahoma, it was about the Oklahoma City bombing and Timothy McVeigh and the tragedy that came with that.

And once we got there, I mean, we didn't realize this, but we were forming a new culture for the whole state of Oklahoma. It was something to feel proud of. It was something to hang on to.

Sports is something that brings everybody together. So I could sense that early. The crowd energy was different -- how loud they were. You go to arenas and you hear the noise level, but this felt a little different to me. The energy ... you could just feel it through the crowd every game. Once (Thunder general manager) Sam Presti and those guys introduced us to the history of the state of Oklahoma and took us to the site where the bombing was and let us know what these people went through and what we're actually planning for it, it made it way more meaningful to go out there and put the jersey on.

ESPN: What do you remember about your first visit to the Oklahoma City National Memorial & Museum?

Durant: [Sam] was really adamant about us touching the community, being outside, going to see the people and feel the people and letting them understand that we were here to stay and that we care about the community. It was powerful. It was powerful. And [the city] has a special place in my heart because of the tragedy it'd been through. And now that we can shed some light on the town and the city and the state, I felt the level of pride that I was from there.

ESPN: You've played in other markets. What makes Oklahoma City different?

Durant: I played in some of the biggest markets, and it felt like coming to those games was just another hobby, something else to do within that city. You got plays, you got Broadway. You've just got so much. It felt like coming to those games was just another hobby, something else to do within that city. You just got so much. You got baseball teams, football teams. Like, it's just something else to add, something else to do.

I felt like going to a Thunder game is ... that was all our people had to do. It was like when the Thunder game was on, I just imagined every small town within Oklahoma that's an hour or two outside of the city shutting down and watching those games.

So being the only sports team there, it felt like we were in college. And I got close with people who came to the games, fans who came to the games. Players were building relationships with people who supported season-ticket holders, people in the front row. It just felt like a family atmosphere, man. It was unique. Once I left and saw how other markets operate, some fans may come to the game halfway through the first quarter. Our fans (in Oklahoma City) were standing up during warmups. It was packed.

That level of enthusiasm for the game of basketball, but also understanding that we're uniting the community at the same time, is pretty dope.

Oklahoma City itself just went through a lot in those times and has always been an overlooked city compared to most cities around the country. And it was that sense of pride. It was just what we wanted to represent -- we're bigger than this. Our city's about love. I know it was a tragedy, a hateful crime that killed a lot of people, but we're a city of love and camaraderie and togetherness.

ESPN: The team's culture has been represented by the ideals of "The Oklahoma Standard," the term for the collective response by the community to the bombing. What did that mean to you during your time there? What do you remember?

Durant: I embodied it every day -- the blue-collar, hard-working, disciplined approach. Sam Presti was the leader in that. When we first got in, everything we did was buttoned up, militant almost. We moved together as a unit. We wore the same things on the plane. You could tell that a team was coming when you saw us pull up to a hotel, came to a game. We were always together as a group.

I can remember early on, our first few years, every time we went on a road trip, we would land and six or seven of us would go through to the mall in every city together -- it's crazy to think about it -- with Oklahoma City Thunder sweats on. But we moved as a unit, and people understood that about us. We were young and energetic. And that matched the franchise in Oklahoma City itself.

The young, new franchise within the NBA -- almost an expansion-like franchise, even though we moved from Seattle. But it felt like an expansion franchise. We had to find our practice facility. First, we were (practicing) in a D2 college. Then we went to the roller rink; they bought that out and renovated that out. So I saw the grind from the ground floor up until where it is now.

Our team and the personalities on our team kind of formed that way. Two young guys that were growing, that were learning, that were in this new city, and the new city was embracing us and vice versa. [The] timing was just perfect when it came to that.

ESPN: You reached your Finals quickly. What was the early success like?

Durant: It was fun because it was unexpected. There was no pressure on us to go win. The pressure was on each one of us individually to get better as players, to become more and more professional. And once we became more and more professional and better individually as players, we always liked playing with each other.

So, once we got on the floor, that was even easier. So once we all got comfortable with the game of basketball, we took off -- and I think our whole organization took off. Sam Presti was a young GM at the time ... so we were all growing at the same time. And we were experiencing things pretty quickly.

So we were hitting these marks early on, and things happened pretty fast for us. And that's from Sam setting the culture where we care strictly about the game and getting better, and everybody -- the coaching staff and the executives -- cared about putting us in a good position to just focus on the game of basketball.

ESPN: When the Thunder won in 2025 and had the parade in downtown Oklahoma City, was there any part of you that was happy for the community to experience that?

Durant: Most definitely. I mean, when we lost in 2012, we almost had like a small parade. So many people came and welcomed us back home and showed us so much love and congratulated us on a great season. I knew at that moment, if the city ever wins a championship, the amount of people that's going to show up for this parade and the energy they're going to have for this parade is going to be insane. ...

I wish our [Thunder] team could have been the one to do it because we were young and we showed we could. But I felt the sense of pride of being an alumni of the Thunder, seeing this team win as well, because I felt that's the evolution of what we did. I felt like Sam Presti hit his final form and figured out the best way for him to be. And Shai and Jalen Williams, I just felt like they all hit that mark, and we kind of laid the foundation on what it meant to be successful young players in this league, and they built upon that.

ESPN: And to see how far the team and city have come with their relationship all these years later, knowing you were there at the start?

Durant: It's one of the most special things that I can say I've been a part of, man. You don't get to be at the infant stages of a lot of things and to see it blossom to where it is now.

And then to also still see some of the people that I work with still there to this day, it's just a testament to everybody that's worked there, that's poured everything into the organization, into the city, and really cared about making the team synonymous with everybody in the city and the state and wanting the community to feel a part of that success. ...

I felt that from the beginning. They were preaching that from the beginning. And to see that culture still going on today, on top of winning a championship and having a good opportunity to keep winning championships? Like I said, I have a sense of pride, man. I really, really am grateful to be an alumni of the Thunder and to help kickstart this thing off with a lot of my teammates.

It's amazing to see ... There's still a little side of me when I play against these guys, I've got a soft spot in my heart for that state."

stories.headline: 2026-27 MLB offseason: Best fits for top free agents
stories.summary: Free agency starts at 5 p.m. ET on Nov. 2. Here are some pairings we'd love to see as this winter gets underway.
stories.body:
While the 2026-27 MLB free agent class is viewed as one of the weakest of the past decade, there is still an interesting list of starting pitchers, one superstar ace and one intriguing breakout player who was one of the league's best hitters in 2026.

Most importantly, with the lockout looming as the collective bargaining agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, there's the potential for a frenetic month of signings leading up to that deadline as teams look to sign players before new rules eventually come into effect.

With the World Series now over and players able to sign starting at 5 p.m. ET on Monday, let's take a look at 10 of the top free agents and their potential best fits.

Tarik Skubal, LHP
2027 age: 30

2026 stats: 12-7, 2.72 ERA, 158.2 IP, 27 BB, 186 SO, 4.6 WAR

Best fit: Chicago Cubs

Kiley McDaniel recently polled MLB insiders to predict the value of Skubal's contract, and the estimates ranged from four years, $176 million all the way up to $500 million, with the average of the 27 projections coming in at eight years and $355 million. That would be the most expensive total value deal ever for a pitcher, surpassing Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal from the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2024 and Gerrit Cole's $324 million deal from the New York Yankees in 2020.

However, there are concerns. Yamamoto was entering his age-25 season and had a history of good health. Cole was entering his age-29 season with just a couple of minor injuries in his past and was coming off three straight 200-inning seasons. Skubal, meanwhile, had Tommy John surgery in college, elbow surgery in 2022 and then the surgery in May of this year to remove loose bodies from his elbow. The minimally invasive procedure allowed for a quick return and Skubal pitched at his Cy Young-level the rest of the season, but teams will be scrutinizing those medical reports.

The other question: Is a starting pitcher worth that kind of investment these days? Yamamoto led the Dodgers to the World Series title in 2025 when he won five games in the postseason and threw two complete games, but that's an outlier performance. The Brewers just rolled to a World Series championship relying much more on their bullpen than their rotation, as the Dodgers did in 2024. It's not that Skubal isn't great -- just that the value of starting pitchers, especially in the postseason, is waning as they throw fewer innings.

With all that said, the Cubs are the perfect fit: a big-market franchise in desperate need of an ace after the rotation ranked 18th in ERA and 21st in strikeout rate. On top of that, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, David Peterson and Matthew Boyd (if he exercises his opt-out) are free agents and every other starter is coming off an injury (Cade Horton will miss most or all of 2027). While the Cubs have room to spend due to all the expired contracts, Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ are also key free agents, so the front office might ultimately decide to spread the money around rather than spend a huge chunk on Skubal.

Another possible fit: St. Louis Cardinals

The Cardinals haven't signed a $100 million free agent since re-signing Matt Holliday in 2010, so this type of move would be out of character for them, but president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom has built a young roster with all kinds of payroll flexibility to make a big splash. According to Cot's Contracts, the Cardinals' estimated 2027 payroll sits at $66 million and the only long-term deal on the books is for JJ Wetherholt. Skubal is the kind of risk they can afford -- and need -- to take.

Yet another possible fit: Los Angeles Dodgers

Yes, we have to mention them. Skubal clearly enjoyed his time in Los Angeles, and this might be the final opportunity for the Dodgers to make one more monster free agent signing before any new CBA rules.

Randy Arozarena, LF
2027 age: 32

2026 stats: .281/.381/.484, 26 HR, 79 RBIs, 5.7 WAR

Best fit: Atlanta Braves/Boston Red Sox

Arozarena had good timing for his walk year: He led the AL in runs scored and posted career highs in WAR, batting average and OPS (not including his 23-game stint in 2020). In fact, his 5.7 WAR is the highest of any of the free agents. He's one of the few good hitters available -- but he's also 32 years old and is limited to left field on defense. Arozarena has reportedly expressed a desire to return to the East Coast.

If that's the case, there are two logical fits in the Braves and Red Sox. Braves left fielders were 27th in OPS while Red Sox left fielders -- mostly Jarren Duran, who had a bad offensive season -- were 26th. The Red Sox can slot a healthy Roman Anthony there, use Arozarena primarily at DH, and look to trade Duran, but that's a lot of roster shuffling. The Braves enter the offseason about $50 million below their 2026 payroll, plus they also need a shortstop -- but Arozarena fills a big hole in the lineup and there isn't a worthy shortstop out there in free agency.

Another possible fit: Philadelphia Phillies

The Phillies need to shake up a lineup that has become too dependent on just Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber and finished 19th in runs and 22nd in OPS. Given Brandon Marsh's second-half collapse and Philly's need for a right-handed hitter, Arozarena makes sense, although he won't help improve a defense that was subpar.

Seiya Suzuki, RF
2027 age: 32

2026 stats: .270/.368/.473, 26 HR, 86 RBIs, 5.1 WAR

Best fit: Toronto Blue Jays

Suzuki was a remarkably consistent hitter during his five years with the Chicago Cubs and had a career high in WAR in 2026 thanks in part to surprisingly outstanding defensive metrics (both DRS and Statcast agreed that he was excellent). Even if the defense was a fluke, he puts runs on the scoreboard with his bat. Chicago's own spending priority this offseason will be its rotation, plus it has options for right field in Kevin Alcantara and Matt Shaw, so re-signing Suzuki wouldn't be the priority.

While the Cubs led the majors in runs, the Blue Jays were last -- and need to upgrade an outfield that fell from seventh in OPS in 2025 to 19th. They're stuck with Anthony Santander's contract for three more years, and Addison Barger missed most of the season after elbow surgery, so a reliable middle-of-the-order hitter is a must. As with Arozarena, Suzuki's age is a concern on a long-term deal, but the Jays are losing $32 million in outfield/DH salary with the departures of free agents George Springer and Myles Straw and can use that to pay Suzuki.

Another possible fit: Detroit Tigers

Tigers right fielders -- Zach McKinstry started the most games there with 49 -- were a collective disaster, hitting .194/.268/.359. It's time to move on from all the temporary fixes and add another lineup anchor. Imagine an outfield of Riley Greene, Max Clark and Suzuki. Detroit's payroll is some $70 million below 2026, so there's room for Suzuki and some pitching additions.

Teruaki Sato, 3B
2027 age: 28

2026 stats: .306/.383/.609, 39 HR, 106 RBIs

Best fit: New York Yankees

The MVP and Triple Crown winner for the Hanshin Tigers of Japan's Central League, Sato's left-handed power makes him one of the most intriguing free agents once he's posted, especially considering the lack of big hitters in free agency. His defense isn't a strength, with some teams perhaps looking at him as a first baseman or outfielder (where he played earlier in his career). He did strike out 164 times in 614 plate appearances, a 26.7% rate similar to Munetaka Murakami's 28.7% rate his final two seasons in Japan. Murakami fanned 35% of the time and hit .207 with the Chicago White Sox this season -- although did launch 35 home runs and walked 92 times.

Sato is hardly a perfect fit for the Yankees -- Ryan McMahon is signed for one more year at $16 million and Sato would add another high-strikeout bat to the lineup, plus a right-handed batter might be a better fit -- but general manager Brian Cashman loves power. Plus, McMahon was wretched at the plate in 2026. A power-hitting trio of Ben Rice, Aaron Judge and Sato could provide 120-plus home runs.

Another possible fit: Seattle Mariners

The Mariners are another team in need of an offensive makeover. Like the Yankees, they need a right-handed hitter more than a lefty, especially since they're likely to lose Arozarena in free agency, but this stat is also staring them in the face: They were last in the majors in OPS, RBIs and runs scored at third base. Brendan Donovan did miss most of the season with injuries but also struggled defensively when he was there; he might be a better fit to replace Arozarena in left field.

Michael King, RHP
2027 age: 32

2026 stats: 12-10, 3.21 ERA, 185 IP, 70 BB, 159 SO, 4.3 WAR

Best fit: San Diego Padres

King is likely to opt out of his $28 million option (he has another one for $30 million in 2028) and try to secure a longer deal after posting a 3.15 ERA over his three years in San Diego's rotation. He did miss time in 2025 with shoulder inflammation, and his strikeout rate has dropped from an excellent 27.7% in 2024 to 21% in 2026, so there are a couple red flags here -- but he's been a steady performer. The Padres need him more than anyone else, with King, Walker Buehler and in-season acquisitions Robbie Ray and Casey Mize all hitting free agency. Without King, the top returning starter is Randy Vasquez.

Another possible fit: Chicago White Sox

As we saw in the postseason when they were trying to piece together their pitching like a Jenga tower, the White Sox need a little help in the rotation. Or a lot of help. They were 26th in ERA, last in innings and 23rd in batting average allowed. They have the young position player core to build around, and maybe Hagen Smith joins the rotation, but they need a veteran starter and have plenty of payroll room to make a major addition.

Jake Bauers, 1B
2027 age: 31

2026 stats: .266/.389/.484, 26 HR, 86 RBIs, 3.3 WAR

Best fit: Milwaukee Brewers

Normally, a breakout season from a 30-year-old would scream "fluke," and that player wouldn't draw much interest in free agency -- but that won't be the case with Bauers. His Statcast page has 90th-plus percentile rankings all over it: expected wOBA, hard-hit rate, bat speed, chase rate, walk rate. That led to a great season in which he hit for power and ranked third in the majors in on-base percentage and 11th in OPS. There was nothing lucky about how he put up those numbers, leading to a belief that he can sustain that high level.

The Brewers aren't normally in the market for 31-year-old free agents, and they do have potential replacements in Andrew Fischer, who led the minors with 48 home runs in reaching Double-A, and Blake Burke, who hit 34 home runs and stole 29 bases in reaching Triple-A. However, Bauers was such a key component of their title run. Both of those prospects also struck out a ton and could use another season in the minors.

Milwaukee also has Andrew Vaughn, who hit .306 this season, in a part-time role. With Vaughn due to make more than $8 million in arbitration, it's unlikely the Brewers would both sign Bauers and bring Vaughn back -- and by the postseason, Bauers was playing every day anyway with Vaughn relegated to the bench. Bauers' track record is limited enough that he shouldn't be priced out of Milwaukee. Look for the Brewers to make a run at re-signing him and then trading Vaughn.

Another possible fit: New York Mets

The Mets let longtime first baseman Pete Alonso walk a year ago and signed Jorge Polanco to replace him. That worked out about as well as a root canal from Dr. Tim Whatley. Polanco is still around, but president of baseball operations David Stearns has indicated the starting rotation and first base would be offseason priorities, making Bauers a possibility for the Mets.

Freddy Peralta, RHP
2027 age: 31

2026 stats: 10-11, 4.42 ERA, 169 IP, 63 BB, 156 SO, 0.7 WAR

Best fit: Chicago White Sox

Fastball Freddy saw his stock dip during a rough four months with the Mets after they acquired him from the Brewers last winter, but then saw it climb back up after a strong finish with the Rays -- a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after coming over at the deadline and then a good postseason. Much was made during the playoffs about the changes Peralta made to get back to his Brewers mechanics, but his strikeout rate was actually lower with the Rays than it was with the Mets. The biggest difference was his batting average on balls in play: .315 with the Mets, .235 with the Rays. His strikeout rate, nearly 31% in 2023, dipped to 21% in 2026. He has been durable, with four consecutive seasons of 30-plus starts, although doesn't often pitch deep into games.

Add it up and it's buyer beware -- although, with five straight seasons with an ERA below 4.00 before 2026, Peralta will be in demand and could receive a nine-figure deal. As mentioned earlier, the White Sox will be looking for rotation help. He's a little homer-prone so isn't necessarily the best match for Guaranteed Rate Field, which is generally home run-friendly, but adding someone who they can pencil in for 30 starts is a huge plus for a young team on the rise.

Another possible fit: Washington Nationals

There are several teams in need of pitching help that could also work here: Nationals, San Francisco Giants, Houston Astros ... we mentioned the Cardinals earlier. Mets? Yeah, that one probably won't happen ... again.

Brandon Lowe, 2B
2027 age: 32

2026 stats: .260/.331/.493, 35 HR, 96 RBIs, 5.4 WAR

Best fit: Pittsburgh Pirates

The majors' most underrated power hitter, Lowe has now hit 30-plus home runs three times, including in both 2025 and 2026, while averaging 35 home runs per 162 games in his career. His big season helped key a dramatic improvement in the Pirates' offense, and his defensive metrics were the best of his career -- 98th percentile in Statcast's outs above average and plus-13 defensive runs saved, which ranked tied for third among second basemen. That helped him produce a career-high 5.4 WAR.

Despite all those glossy numbers, Lowe's age and injury history -- he averaged 94 games a season from 2022 to 2024 -- should keep his contract down to a level where the Pirates can afford to re-sign him. And they should want to bring him back. There are also other second basemen available on the market in Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Luis Arraez, another reason Lowe should remain affordable.

Another possible fit: San Francisco Giants

The Giants have several highly rated infielders in the lower minors -- Josuar Gonzalez, Luis Hernandez, Jhonny Level -- but they're a few years away. Arraez was their second baseman until they traded him, and while they got Marcelo Mayer in the Erik Miller trade with the Red Sox, Mayer hasn't shown much at the plate during his 380 plate appearances in the majors.

Adrian Morejon, LHP
2027 age: 28

2026 stats: 9-3, 2.83 ERA, 86 IP, 28 BB, 107 SO, 1.9 WAR

Best fit: Philadelphia Phillies

One of the elite relievers in the game, Morejon has a 2.58 ERA over the past three seasons while leading all relievers in innings pitched and ranking seventh in strikeouts. Firing 99-mph fastballs with an outstanding changeup from the left side, he increased his strikeout rate to a career-high 30.4% in 2026 while pitching 86 innings. He was already going to be in demand as a left-handed high-leverage reliever, but even more so after watching the Brewers' bullpen dominate the postseason with three lefty relievers.

The Phillies are set at closer with Jhoan Duran, but the rest of the bullpen is a mess, finishing 21st in ERA. Jose Alvarado has been their longtime top southpaw, but he's a free agent and coming off a bad season (5.86 ERA). Phillies lefty relievers allowed an .805 OPS, second worst in the majors. Give Duran some help.

Another possible fit: Chicago Cubs

Morejon is a fit for almost every team, so let's throw the Cubs out here again as they try to figure out how they can chase down their division rivals. They saw 14 different relievers record saves in 2026, and their lefty relievers ranked 21st in OPS allowed and 25th in strikeout rate. Morejon would give them a workhorse setup guy or a potential closer.

Nick Martinez, RHP
2027 age: 36

2026 stats: 15-6, 3.10 ERA, 180 IP, 26 BB, 109 SO, 3.9 WAR

Best fit: Arizona Diamondbacks

Martinez has a $20 million mutual option but will likely opt out and aim for a multiyear deal after an All-Star season with the Rays. It will be interesting to see how teams view him given his low strikeout rate and age, but he's been a durable swingman in the past and then delivered 180 innings as a full-time starter for the Rays in 2026. They had him use his changeup and sinker more, and he relies on great control and soft contact to outperform his strikeout numbers.

Since there are more balls in play when he pitches, he's a better fit for a team with good defense -- and one who won't be playing in the more expensive Skubal/King/Peralta market. The Diamondbacks could fit here, although after ranking 29th in rotation strikeout rate, they might be wary about adding another low-whiff starter. But they do need to replace Zac Gallen.

Another possible fit: Tampa Bay Rays

The Rays paid Martinez $9 million in 2026, so a deal that would more than double that salary might put them in an uncomfortable zone. But with Shane McClanahan and Griffin Jax both due for free agency after the 2027 season and a lack of starting pitching prospects in the upper minors, Tampa Bay might want to lock down Martinez into the future given how well it worked for both sides this past season.

stories.headline: Valkyries and Dream meet one more time in winner-take-all in the WNBA Finals
stories.summary: On Halloween, what will decide whether Golden State or Atlanta wins its first title in the WNBA's first Game 7?
stories.byline: Kendra Andrews and Kareem Copeland and Alexa Philippou and Michael Voepel
stories.body:
The Dream and Valkyries have stretched the season as long as it can go, until the last day in October. This year, Halloween will bring a championship trophy to one franchise in the WNBA's first Game 7 as Golden State hosts Atlanta on Saturday (8 p.m. ET).

The first Game 6 went to Atlanta 80-69 on Thursday at State Farm Arena to even the WNBA Finals at 3-3. The league moved to a best-of-seven format for the Finals last season, but the Las Vegas Aces swept the Phoenix Mercury. This year, we're going the distance.

Both teams have won twice at home and once on the road. The No. 2 seed Valkyries, whose passionate fanbase has turned Ballhalla into a legendary venue in just the franchise's second season, hope to celebrate at home. The No. 4 seed Dream, who were swept in three previous Finals appearances, want to take the prize back to Atlanta.

We've seen three games in this series in which Golden State's defense had the last word and three when Atlanta's offense has busted past the 70-point mark. That has been the line in the sand: When the Dream have scored below 70, they've lost.

Since many Golden State fans already show up in Valkyries costumes, Halloween night at Chase Center might not look that different from another game. But it will feel like the biggest night in both franchises' history. Both seek their first championship.

ESPN looks at what could determine the champ or derail the dream.

How does Golden State bounce back from Game 6, especially Atlanta's 32-point first quarter?

Kendra Andrews: While Golden State coach Natalie Nakase called her team's tough start to Game 6 "unacceptable," guard Veronica Burton focused on the positive. She gave the Valkyries props for battling from as far down as 25 points to pull within eight toward the end of the game.

"At the end of the day, we feel good," Burton said. But under the silver lining, the Valkyries' tenor sounded more agitated than we've heard in the past.

Tip your cap to the Valkyries for at least applying a little pressure to the Dream's utter dominance -- which Burton pointed out that Golden State failed to do in its other two losses. After dropping Games 2 and 3, the Valkyries had what they've said were brutally honest conversations with one another, holding everyone accountable for their mistakes and finding their fight. Nakase has encouraged her players to correct her when they believe her game plan is not working, always looking for ways she can improve communication about what she needs from her players. Expect them to do the same heading into Saturday.

Before Game 6, Nakase complimented her team's composure, and that will be what it relies on in Game 7.

Kareem Copeland: The Valkyries have never felt like a team with wide emotional swings. Sure, there was disappointment with the way they played in Game 6, but there were similar feelings after losses in Games 2 and 3 before answering with two consecutive wins to grab control of the series. Burton even said "we quit" in Games 2 and 3. Still, Golden State showed the ability to shake off losses and deficits already in this series without being emotionally shaken. And physical play hasn't really seemed like a significant concern for the 2026 Valkyries.

Michael Voepel: Realistically, the Valkyries knew Game 6 on the road after winning the previous two games was a tall order. Atlanta had lost back-to-back games just once this season: during the Dream's only slump, a five-game losing streak from June 24 to July 4. The idea of Atlanta falling three times in a row in the playoffs was too much to ask from even the Valkyries' vaunted defense. So even though they would have loved to have packed up the trophy Thursday, the Valkyries are not going into Game 7 dispirited.

Philippou: Game 6 was deflating for the Valkyries, but Nakase has said her team consistently learns from its losses and thrives with its back against the wall. Given the Valkyries actually outscored the Dream by six in the final 30 minutes on Thursday, being overly defeated about Game 6 would be foolish.

What will decide Game 7?

Copeland: Once again: turnovers, turnover differential, points off turnovers. That has been the biggest predictor of success in a low-scoring series where every possession is overly valuable. Game 6 didn't hold up in that way in the final numbers, but when the Dream built a 20-point halftime lead, they scored 21.7% of their points off turnovers. The Valkyries forced 10 second-half turnovers when they rallied.

Philippou: Which team dictates the pace. The Dream fared so much better Thursday when they were able to push the ball up the floor and capitalize in transition or with early offense. The Valkyries, on the other hand, thrive when they can slow the game and turn things into more of a rock fight.

"Today we made it very intentional to get out, push the pace, get to the corners, spreading the ball around, having that ball movement, creating as much space as we can for our team," Atlanta point guard Jordin Canada said postgame.

Dream coach Karl Smesko echoed Canada in the news conference: "I think the biggest problem is when we're not playing at our pace, and if the game is at their pace, they have an advantage. If the game is at our pace, we have an advantage. We have to be just locked in to the way we play, and we can't let them take us out of that.

"I think that will be the challenge in Game 7 for both teams, probably."

Voepel: Whichever team is less haunted by its mistakes. The weight of every play gets a little heavier for everyone in a Game 7. Both teams are in the exact same position, and composure matters from the tip. Missed shots, bad passes, foul calls all take on more meaning because so much is on the line. The Valkyries like the game best when it's gritty and even a bit ugly because that means they are dictating the pace and frustrating the opponents' offense. The Dream want to see shots go down early, as that has had an impact on their confidence.

What one player is the biggest X factor for determining Game 7?

Copeland: The Dream have struggled to score in each of their losses. In the Game 6 victory, Allisha Gray looked like her healthy self as the team sprinted out to a 46-point first half. A low-scoring slugfest isn't Atlanta's advantage against this particular opponent, so it needs to put points up. Gray was the No. 9 scorer in the league during the regular season and averaged 22.0 points in the first round before that finger/hand injury suffered in Game 1 of the semifinals sidelined her for the rest of that series. She combined for 15 points in losses in Games 4 and 5 and dropped 23 in Game 6. Can a four-time All-Star be considered an X factor? She should be.

Philippou: Kiah Stokes -- the so-called Warden of Valcatraz by Golden State fans -- looked like the potential Finals MVP after Game 5, but in Game 6 she only saw the floor for 20 minutes, with Nakase opting to go with Laeticia Amihere for her first meaningful minutes since Game 1. Nakase said she thought Stokes' legs weren't moving as well as Amihere's. Even though Angel Reese was relatively contained -- she finished with 15 points on 5-for-18 shooting but stepped up as a playmaker with six assists -- the Valkyries have been at their best this series when Stokes has been able to win that matchup. With her relentlessness, Reese is tempting to take in a winner-take-all championship setting; Stokes, meanwhile, has the edge in experience as a three-time champion. It'll be a fascinating matchup to watch unfold.

Voepel: There's one No. 1 draft pick on the floor in this series: Dream guard Rhyne Howard. The 2022 top pick and Rookie of the Year, Howard has scored in double figures in all but one game in this series. In the past two, she has combined for 41 points on 50% shooting (13 of 26) from the field. Howard was a big part of the Dream's lethal first quarter Thursday and will look to do the same Saturday. But it won't be easy, as Gabby Williams, Burton and the rest of the Valkyries defense will throw their best at her. And it should be noted that Williams also has scored in double figures in all but one game this series.

Golden State is 2-1 at Chase Center in the Finals. Will home-court advantage play a factor in Game 7?

Andrews: Expect Chase to be otherworldly Saturday night. Ballhalla on Halloween with a title at stake? It will be impossible to hear anything. So, yes, of course it will give the Valkyries an advantage.

But the Dream have spoken about how they like to play there, in such an elite basketball environment. After Game 6, Reese said having played there three times throughout this series -- one of which Atlanta won -- helps prepare them for this moment.

"I think that the crowd doesn't really get to us much, but I think, obviously, Game 7 is going to be a lot louder," Reese said. "The energy is going to be electric in there."

The Dream have to make sure their communication has little to no error, and they don't let the Valkyries get off to a hot start to get the building rocking.

Voepel: As mentioned, this is the second year of the best-of-seven format and the first time it will go all seven games. But history favors the host Valkyries based on results from best-of-five WNBA Finals series. The WNBA moved to that format in 2005, and it went the distance eight times. The home team won six of those, most recently with New York in 2024. The exceptions were in 2007, when Phoenix claimed Game 5 at Detroit, and 2016, when Los Angeles won Game 5 at Minnesota.

stories.headline: Messi eligible for crunch Miami game with Revs despite yellow card haul
stories.summary: Lionel Messi is eligible for Inter Miami's game against the New England Revolution on Sunday despite receiving his fifth yellow card of the season on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi is eligible for Inter Miami CF's match against the New England Revolution on Sunday despite receiving his fifth yellow card of the season on Wednesday.

Messi received a yellow card in the 44th minute of Miami's 2-2 draw with FC Cincinnati on Wednesday at Nu Stadium, taking his total for the season to five. The Inter Miami captain was also booked during match weeks eight, 11, 20, 31 and 33.

MLS rules state that a player will "automatically reduce his yellow card accumulation total by one yellow card each time he appears in five consecutive matches without receiving a yellow card, red card or supplemental discipline in such matches."

The league's "good behavior incentive" is applied a maximum of three times throughout the regular season.

Messi went more than five games without receiving a yellow card, pardoning his previous yellow card. Though the yellow card will remain on Messi's disciplinary record, the booking no longer counts towards the amount that would force him to face a suspension.

Inter Miami head coach Cristian González said the team no longer has a margin of error when it comes to dropping points during the regular season as they chase Concacaf Champions Cup qualification.

"I am convinced that the frustration we're feeling, much like after the previous match, must make us stronger, because we no longer have any margin for error," González said Wednesday after the draw with Cincinnati. "We need to realize that we are a club that must step up, take risks, be bold, and play football without the fear of making mistakes."

Inter Miami sits in third place in the Eastern Conference, just two points behind the Revs.

Regardless of the outcome, the Herons and Revs have both already qualified for the 2026 MLS playoffs, but Miami's spot in next season's Champions Cup will depend in large part on Sunday's match.

The winners of MLS Cup, the Leagues Cup, U.S. Open Cup, MLS Supporters' Shield and the league's Eastern and Western Conference champions each get a spot in the Champions Cup. With Nashville having secured the Supporters' Shield, second place in the East will get one of the automatic spots, making this penultimate game of the season crucial for the two sides.

stories.headline: Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues
stories.summary: We're a quarter of the way through the 2026-27 European season -- long enough to separate fact from fiction when it comes to from. Who's been lucky? Who's been good? Who's been both, or neither?
stories.body:
About a quarter of the way through the club season, your place in the table only means so much. In the Premier League and Bundesliga, 14 teams -- including Ipswich Town, Paderborn and even Tottenham Hotspur -- are within six points of the top four. In Ligue 1, it's 13. In LaLiga, 14 teams are within six points of the relegation zone. You can find some separation here and there, but we're just getting started, and we only have a partial picture of how things will end up.

We also know that the table is lying a little bit. We see funky results all the time, and they have an outsized impact when we're seen only a small portion of matches. Still, by this point in the 2026-27 campaign, each Big Five team has played hundreds and hundreds of possessions, and we know who is creating (or allowing) the best chances. Thanks to xG, we also know what that means.

Essentially, xG is a chance creation metric. It obviously doesn't guarantee success, especially in the short term, but over the long haul a team's ability to create superior shot quality and/or volume is more predictive than simply who's putting the ball in the net in a small sample. And by comparing who's generated the most points to who's created chance creation advantages, with a fun trend line in between, we can get a grasp of who is ahead of or behind where they should be.

Who's both lucky and good? Who's good, but unlucky? Who's the opposite?

Here are some xG standouts, for better or worse, in Europe's Big Five leagues.

- Jones: Vozinha's Ballon d'Or appearance was made for us

- Ogden: Man United are a mess. Where are the Glazers?

- Olley: Ballon d'Or is Kane's crowning moment

Lucky and good

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game, but more points than expected

Lazio. Lazio have finished seventh or worse in Serie A for three straight years, and due to an ongoing fan protest of club president Claudio Lotito, they're averaging a league-worst home attendance of 9,515. They've also only dropped two points in nine league matches, and they're tied with Inter atop the table. Pretty wild stuff.

It's also probably unsustainable stuff.

While they've enjoyed a few genuinely dominant performances (like a 6-2 win at Sassuolo), they've also scored 22 goals from shots worth just 15.5 xG. Forward Tijjani Noslin, winger Gustav Isaksen and midfielder Kenneth Taylor have combined for nine goals from 3.9 xG; I probably don't have to spell out how unsustainable that is. Lazio have stockpiled enough points to remain in the Champions League hunt for a while, but there's a goal-scoring slump in their future, whether or not there are fans in the stands to see it.

Atletico Madrid. Diego Simeone scoffs at your advanced stats. Over the past 12 full seasons, Atletico have produced a goal differential higher -- and in some cases, much higher -- than their xG differential 11 times. In fact, over the Simeone era, their GD in league play (+504) is 46% higher than their xGD (+346.0). Dark magic is a real thing, I guess.

Atleti have always been happy allowing opponents to hammer shots into a box cluttered by defenders (with the immaculate Jan Oblak behind them), and they've always had impressive finishers -- Antoine Griezmann (143 goals from 113.6 xG) and Angel Correa (68 from 57.4) in particular -- ready to turn a half-chance into a goal. But even without either Griezmann or Correa, they're overachieving again this fall. Oblak remains excellent, Álex Baena has picked up the "major finishing overachiever" mantle, and in four matches with a negative xG differential, Atleti have scored two wins, a draw and only one loss.

Manchester City. No one else has been Lazio-level lucky this season, but City damn near packed a season's worth of xG fortune into one match -- a 5-3 win over Sunderland in which they generated 2.8 xG and allowed 3.6. It was their only match with a negative xG differential this season, but between that and a 1-0 win over Manchester United (xGD: +0.1), they could have easily dropped more points than they actually have this season.

They have an xG cheat code in habitually excellent finisher Erling Haaland (nine goals from shots worth 6.1), but they've been lucky that their defense (seventh in xG allowed) hasn't been more costly.

Borussia Dortmund. It's been difficult to get a read on BVB this season. They've generated a positive xG differential in all seven Bundesliga matches, and their only losses have come against Bayern in the Franz Beckenbauer Super Cup and at Bodø/Glimt in their North Pole fortress in the Champions League. But after winning six straight before the international break, they sandwiched a pair of frustrating draws around the Bodø/Glimt loss upon their return.

Dortmund are on the lucky-and-good list because their defense has been a bit too successful. They've allowed goals in just two Bundesliga matches, and their four goals allowed have come from shots worth 7.3 xG. Yes, they have a high-level goalkeeper in Gregor Kobel, but opponents have simply missed the target quite a bit, too. That likely won't continue, nor will their current tie with Bayern in the league table.

Como. Como are easily Serie A's happiest Champions League story thus far, having won two of their first three matches in their debut in the competition. In theory, they've balanced those duties with solid league play, too -- they're fourth in the league and only five points from first. But they've been at least a little bit fortunate: They've suffered a negative xG differential in four of nine Serie A matches, but they've won two of those four and drawn in one.

- Who are Como? The vacation-destination club that just rocked Man United

That said, the trends are strong: Since returning from the international break, they've suffered a negative xGD only once and have taken 10 points from four league matches. Including their Champions League stomping of Manchester United, they've generated an xGD of at least plus-1.1 in three straight. They were lucky and good, but they might just be good now.

Good, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Nottingham Forest. If you didn't look at the table, you'd think Oliver Glasner is doing great work in his first season as manager in Nottingham. Forest beat Aston Villa and drew with Liverpool at Anfield, and for the season they're sixth in xG created (13.4), second in xG allowed (9.0) and fifth in overall xG differential. The fundamentals are in great shape.

Somehow they're also 18th in the table, behind even Glasner's direction-less former employer, Crystal Palace. They've turned shots worth 13.4 xG into only six goals; attackers Morgan Gibbs-White, Liam Delap and Chris Wood have attempted 38 shots worth 5.3 xG, but they've put only eight shots on target and scored twice. Forest have generated a positive xG differential in six of eight matches and have somehow won just one of them. That they will almost certainly right the ship in this regard and start winning matches soon, but how many unnecessary points will they have dropped by then?

Brest. After surging to third in Ligue 1 in 2023-24 and qualifying for the Champions League, Brest slipped to ninth and then 12th in the last two seasons. Now they're 13th. It appears the balloon is losing helium.

If the results start matching the chance creation, however, a turnaround is possible. They're second in Ligue 1 in xG differential, well behind PSG but well ahead of everyone else. They've created a dominant xG differential of +1.9 or better in four matches but have somehow won only one of them. Both their finishing and defense have let them down at times, but midfielder Joris Chotard is fifth in the league in chances created, and the combo of young wingers Kamory Doumbia and Pathé Mboup with veteran big man Ludovic Ajorque has created a number of dangerous opportunities.

This is one of France's better teams, no matter what the table says.

Villarreal. Villarreal are third in xG differential and 10th in LaLiga. They have dropped unlikely points to Atletico Madrid (2-2 draw, +2.8 xG differential), Elche (0-0 draw, +2.1 xGD) and Alaves (1-0 loss, +1.0). Forwards Georges Mikautadze and Ayoze Pérez have scored just four goals from shots worth 8.4 xG; in the Champions League, meanwhile, they've scored two goals from 1.2.

Aside from finishing, there's nothing inherently wrong with this squad. They're third in shots per possession margin and fourth in xG per shot margin. They play a pretty possession game -- Renato Veiga is one of only two players in LaLiga (along with Barcelona's Gerard Martín) to already have over 100 progressive passes and 100 progressive carries -- without giving up much on the counter. But they're eight points behind fourth-place Real Betis; they have some ground to make up.

Bournemouth. Only Manchester City, Arsenal and Brentford have led more Premier League matches this season than Bournemouth, but somehow the Cherries have turned leads in six matches -- and positive xG differentials in six matches -- into just two wins. Marcus Tavernier has scored a lovely five goals from shots worth 3.6 xG, but the rest of the team has just six goals from shots worth 10.9. They aren't generating the sizable advantages they should, and they've been outscored 4-0 from the 80th minute on. They're third in xG differential but 13th in the table because of the late leaks.

It could be worse -- most of their unfortunate results have been draws and not losses. But with so many bigger clubs struggling out of the gate, Bournemouth had a chance to establish a good spot in the race for a top-five finish. They're off of that pace.

Bayern Munich. Maybe one day this hard-luck club will catch a break. Alas, the 35-time German champions have dropped points twice -- 0-0 at Schalke (xG differential: +1.7), 2-2 at Augsburg (+2.5) -- despite dominating the early stages of the season as much as ever.

Seriously, though, this is ridiculous:

Every so often, the Bundesliga figures out how to balance great crowds, fun stories and sustained challenges for Bayern, but it doesn't appear this will be one of those years, even if those two draws mean Bayern and Borussia Dortmund are tied in points at the moment. Bayern's xGD is actually higher now than it was after they won their first seven matches last season.

Ballon d'Or winner (!) Harry Kane has gone through his version of a finishing funk (he has four league goals from shots worth 5.2 xG), and Serge Gnabry is in a similar boat (one goal from 2.2 xG). Something tells me they'll be all right.

Bad, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Venezia. It's a yo-yo period in Venice. Venezia were promoted from Serie B in 2021, but went straight back down. They came back up in 2024, went back down in 2025, then came right back up in 2026. And through eight matchdays, they have three points and are last in the Serie A table.

However, they haven't been that bad. This team obviously isn't loaded with proven finishers, but scoring just six goals from shots worth 14.5 xG is severely unfortunate. Forwards John Yeboah, Albion Rrahmani and Lion Lauberbach somehow have one goal from 5.1 xG; they aren't generating ridiculously high-quality shots, but that is still some unsustainably poor finishing. Venezia have generated a positive xG differential in four of nine matches, and they're 14th overall in xGD. They'll have a chance to stay up if their finishing begins to reflect their actual chance creation.

Borussia Mönchengladbach. The five-time German champions finally notched a win last weekend, shocking Stuttgart 3-2. It was both deserving and a long time coming. They had lost their first six league matches, alternating between awful (losing to RB Leipzig and Freiburg by a combined 8-0) and unlucky (4-3 losses to Elversberg and Mainz despite a combined xGD of +0.5).

The club hired former St. Pauli manager Alexander Blessin on Sept. 22, and while he made an immediate impact on their defense, they finally generated some offense in Stuttgart too. American right midfielder Joe Scally and 17-year old left midfielder Wael Mohya each had a goal and an assist in that match, and if Gladbach can generate production like that from the wings, maybe it will offset the black hole of production they've gotten from their center forwards in the absence of injured veteran Tim Kleindienst.

Valencia. After pulling nine points from their first 11 league matches last year and 10 from their first 15 in 2024-25, Valencia have just six points after 10 matches this season. Only Villarreal and Osasuna have been worse at finishing the season: Valencia have turned shots worth 10.8 xG into only seven goals. In matches against Real Betis (1-0 loss), Celta Vigo (0-0 draw) and Athletic Club (0-0 draw) they attempted 40 shots worth 3.3 xG, and none went in the net. Those matches could have easily produced six to nine points ... but yielded just two instead.

Despite average defensive numbers, there's no way to say this team is anything better than below average. But while they're growing awfully familiar to relegation scraps at the moment -- and if you play with fire enough, you will get burned -- I can't say they're actually relegation-worthy just yet.

Troyes. Back in Ligue 1 after a three-year absence, Troyes attempt more shots than their opponents and press frequently. They don't attempt many good shots, but they rank 15th in xG created and 10th in xG allowed. That they only have five points from eight matches is therefore a smidgen unlucky. They've scored only five goals from shots worth 9.7 xG, and they've allowed 16 goals from shots worth 13.2. A lot of that damage comes from one match -- a 6-2 loss to Strasbourg in which both teams generated 2.9 xG -- but forwards Renaud Ripart and Jeremy Le Douaron have combined for two goals on 4.7 xG. Finish at more normal levels, and they'll have a solid shot at survival.

Sunderland. Sunderland were the "stats don't matter" team of 2025-26, ranking 18th in the Premier League in xG differential, but somehow finishing seventh and grabbing a spot in the Europa League. You usually don't have to wait long for what we'll call statistical comeuppance. This year they've actually improved to 15th in xG differential, and they've generated a positive xGD in four of eight matches, but they've won just one because aside from Brian Brobbey (three goals from shots worth 3.2 xG), no one can turn shots into goals.

Sunderland rank third in the league in xG per shot, but they're 18th in goals and haven't scored in a league match since Sept. 20. That puts them at the bottom of the table. A lot of teams are struggling at the moment, so they're not in too big a hole, but after this weekend's trip to Coventry City, their schedule gets awfully tricky.

Lucky and bad

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game but more points than expected

Frosinone. Frosinone have been promoted to Serie A four times since 2015; they have yet to avoid going straight back down. That they're currently sixth in points per game, ahead of mighty Juventus, is a thrilling story. But it's really hard to believe this story will last. They're also 18th in xG differential, having scored 17 goals from shots worth 13.1 xG while allowing 13 goals from shots worth 19.5.

This is unsustainable in obvious ways, but as Sunderland learned last year, if you stockpile points early, you can ride it out when regression to the mean invariably hits. They're already nine points above the drop zone with a game in hand; from here, it won't take too much additional good fortune for them to survive a year in Serie A for the first time.

Elversberg. The most delightful early Bundesliga story is also a fortunate one. Tiny Elversberg, from a town of 13,000 people, have three wins and 10 points from seven matches in their top-division debut. They're a healthy eighth in the table, but they also have yet to actually generate a positive xG differential in a match, and in three one-goal wins they scored 11 goals from shots worth 7.4 xG.

This is an optimistic team with fun attacking ideas, and maybe they can continue to avoid the relegation hunt with bursts of excellence from players such as 22-year-old David Mokwa (1.2 xG, two goals) and 21-year-old Maurice Krattenmacher (2.4 xG, three goals). But they lost 4-0 to RB Leipzig last weekend, and it feels like there might be a few more heavy defeats in their future. Hopefully I'm wrong.

Marseille. Not only are Marseille a terribly disappointing eighth in Ligue 1 at the moment, but they're lucky to even be that high. Their 18 goals scored (first in the league) have come from just 13.6 xG (seventh), while their 18.5 xG allowed (last) has turned into only 13 goals (11th). Last week's 4-3 win over Le Havre featured a minus-1.6 xG differential.

Only Strasbourg have a lower league xG differential than l'OM right now. Marseille do have historically solid finishers like Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão pacing the attack, and a lot of their defensive overachievement came from a single match -- a 2-1 loss to PSG in which they allowed shots worth 5.1 xG. Still, the fundamentals do not suggest that manager Bruno Genesio is fielding a team worth a spot in a European competition at the moment.

Cagliari. Like Frosinone, Cagliari has stocked up on some early points (13 in nine Serie A matches) thanks to some early good fortune. They've suffered a negative xG differential in six of nine matches, but have won two of those with a draw. They've gotten spectacular goalkeeping from Elia Caprile thus far, but allowing just 13 goals from shots worth 17.3 xG is pretty fortunate.

Strangely, though, it's offset some poor finishing from Cagliari, too: While left winger Daniel Maldini is on a hot streak (five goals from shots worth 3.4 xG), the rest of the team has just three goals from 8.1 xG, and if their own finishing progresses more than opponents', they could remain mid-table for quite a while longer.

Newcastle United. Let's isolate that PPG vs. xGD chart above with just Premier League teams.

Maybe no attack in Europe has defied xG more than Newcastle's, and in two different directions.

- Yoane Wissa: 1 goal from shots worth 3.0 xG (minus-2.0 difference)

- Everyone else: 11 goals from shots worth 6.2 xG (plus-4.8 difference)

Wissa has done a great job of generating nearly one-third of Newcastle's xG by himself, but he's been in a major finishing slump. And it's been more than offset by the fact that other guys can't seem to miss.

Newcastle ranks 16th in shots per possession margin and 19th in xG per shot margin; they've generated a positive xG differential in only one match, but incredibly, they lost that match and have only lost two of seven with a negative xGD. It either works (two of three wins were by two goals) or really, really doesn't (two of three losses were by three goals). And I honestly don't have much of an idea of what to expect from them moving forward. I'm not incredibly optimistic, though.
